newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada urges Brazilian president on prisoner deal.
newsitem.headline: Canada urges Brazilian president on prisoner deal.

text.p: The leaders of Brazil and Canada on Tuesday discussed a prisoner exchange agreement which could allow two Canadians convicted in the 1989 kidnapping of a Brazilian businessman to return to Canada.

But Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said he would not sign the treaty until similar agreements were reached with other countries, and he also had to take Brazilian public opinion into account.
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien told reporters he had urged Cardoso to proceed without delay on the issue, but he understood the sensitivity of the situation.

Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said: "They're negotiating with us and with other countries for an exchange of prisoners treaty ... Once they get a grouping of these treaties together then we can proceed."

He said an agreement would allow for the return to Canada of people like Christine Lamont and her fiance David Spencer, serving a 28-year prison sentence for the kidnapping of Brazilian millionaire Abilio Diniz.
The couple had argued in a Brazilian court that the kidnapping, as part of a left-wing guerrilla tactic for a $30 million ransom, was a political and not a common crime.

Because they had been convicted as common criminals, Lamont, 38, and Spencer, 34, got 28 years instead of five to 10 years normally doled out for a political crime, Lamont's mother Marilyn told reporters in Ottawa.
Axworthy said pursuing the treaty was "the most effective means of seeking their release."

The agreement has been waiting to be approved by Cardoso, who said: "It's not a matter of agreement ... Now we have to take into account not just the Canadians but the different nationalities that are in prison."
If the treaty is ratified, Lamont and Spencer would apply to serve their sentence in Canada, where they could appeal their conviction and be released earlier.
